A1-A2.headline: How German Lands Tried to Become One Country

pages.text: Have you ever wondered how Germany became one country? Long ago, it was not one nation. From 1815 to 1866, there were about thirty-seven separate German-speaking states. Many people wanted to join together to make one big, strong country.
pages.caption: A cartoon showing German unity.

evidence.articleCaption: German unity as fiasco with each state viewing itself separate. Cartoon from Münchner Leuchtkugeln, 1848.Caption reads: "German Unity. A Tragedy in one Act."

pages.text: These lands had many different rulers and independent governments. Even though the people spoke the same language, they did not share a single national leader. Leaders and citizens started to discuss how they could bring all these separate regions together into one powerful country.

Politicians created two main plans to solve this problem. The Greater German solution wanted to include all German-speaking lands, led by the Austrian Empire. The Lesser German solution wanted to include only northern states without Austria, led by the Kingdom of Prussia.
pages.caption: Map showing Prussian expansion.

imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Adam Carr at English Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 3.0)

evidence.articleCaption: Prussia's expansion into the German Empire from 1807 (dark blue): green territories added according to the 1815 Congress of Vienna, light blue territories after the Austro-Prussian War of 1866. Yellow territories joined the German Empire in 1871 after the Franco-Prussian War.

pages.text: The debate over these two plans caused serious political arguments and even wars. After Austria lost a major war against Prussia in 1866, the competition ended. In 1871, the Lesser German solution won, and Prussia successfully created a new German Empire without Austria.

Even after the new empire formed, the idea of bringing all German speakers together remained popular. Years later, after World War I, some people tried again to join Austria with Germany, but international treaties stopped them from doing so.

B1-B2.headline: The Great Debate Over Nineteenth-Century German Unification

pages.text: How did a collection of independent states become a single nation? During the nineteenth century, political thinkers debated the German question. Between 1815 and 1866, roughly thirty-seven independent states formed the German Confederation. Rising nationalism inspired citizens to demand a single nation-state for people who shared a common language.
pages.caption: A satirical 1848 cartoon.

evidence.articleCaption: German unity as fiasco with each state viewing itself separate. Cartoon from Münchner Leuchtkugeln, 1848.Caption reads: "German Unity. A Tragedy in one Act."

pages.text: Political geography in the region was highly fragmented. Centuries of decentralized authority left numerous kingdoms, duchies, and principalities, each ruled by an independent sovereign. Furthermore, religious differences strongly influenced political loyalties. Catholic regions mostly favored Austria, while Protestant regions preferred leadership under Prussia.

In 1848, a wave of revolutions led to the formation of the Frankfurt Parliament. The assembly debated two competing proposals. The Greater German solution aimed to unify all German speakers under Austrian leadership. Conversely, the Lesser German solution proposed a northern nation led by Prussia, excluding Austria entirely.
pages.caption: Map illustrating Prussian growth.

imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Adam Carr at English Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 3.0)

evidence.articleCaption: Prussia's expansion into the German Empire from 1807 (dark blue): green territories added according to the 1815 Congress of Vienna, light blue territories after the Austro-Prussian War of 1866. Yellow territories joined the German Empire in 1871 after the Franco-Prussian War.

pages.text: Although the Frankfurt Parliament offered the imperial crown to the Prussian king in 1849, he refused it, and the initial revolution failed. However, political maneuvers continued under leaders like Otto von Bismarck. After Austria suffered a decisive defeat in the Austro-Prussian War of 1866, the conflict was finally resolved.

The Lesser German solution ultimately prevailed in 1871. Following successful military campaigns, Prussia united the remaining German states into a powerful new empire. Austria-Hungary remained excluded from this new national entity, marking the definitive settlement of the historical German question.

C1-C2.headline: Navigating the German Question and Nineteenth-Century Statecraft

pages.text: The nineteenth-century geopolitical discourse surrounding the German question encapsulated a profound struggle over national identity and territorial reorganization. Between 1815 and 1866, approximately thirty-seven sovereign political entities constituted the German Confederation. Catalyzed by contemporary nationalist movements, intellectuals and revolutionaries sought to consolidate German-speaking populations into a cohesive nation-state.
pages.caption: An 1848 political cartoon.

evidence.articleCaption: German unity as fiasco with each state viewing itself separate. Cartoon from Münchner Leuchtkugeln, 1848.Caption reads: "German Unity. A Tragedy in one Act."

pages.text: The structural legacy of the Holy Roman Empire left Central Europe politically fractured into absolute principalities and grand duchies. Religious allegiance played a pivotal role in shaping factional alignment; predominantly Catholic southern states gravitated toward the Habsburg monarchy, whereas northern Protestant territories aligned with the rising power of Prussia under the House of Hohenzollern.

During the 1848 revolutions, the Frankfurt Parliament became the epicenter of constitutional debate. The assembly confronted two mutually exclusive paradigms: the Großdeutsche Lösung, advocating for a pan-German state led by Austria, and the Kleindeutsche Lösung, championing a Prussian-led northern union. However, Austria presented a complex demographic dilemma due to its extensive non-German territories and reluctance to dismantle its multiethnic empire.
pages.caption: Map depicting Prussian influence.

imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Adam Carr at English Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 3.0)

evidence.articleCaption: Prussia's expansion into the German Empire from 1807 (dark blue): green territories added according to the 1815 Congress of Vienna, light blue territories after the Austro-Prussian War of 1866. Yellow territories joined the German Empire in 1871 after the Franco-Prussian War.

pages.text: Although the Frankfurt parliament tendered the imperial crown to Prussian King Frederick William IV in 1849, the monarch demurred, precipitating the immediate collapse of the revolutionary assembly. Subsequent diplomatic and military maneuvers by Otto von Bismarck systematically marginalized Austrian influence. The decisive Austro-Prussian War of 1866 effectively shattered Vienna's hegemony over German affairs.

The definitive resolution materialized in 1871 through the establishment of the German Empire under Prussian dominance, cementing the Lesser German solution. Although irredentist aspirations resurfaced following the dissolution of Austria-Hungary after World War I, international covenants such as the Treaty of Versailles explicitly prohibited territorial incorporation, illustrating the enduring and contentious legacy of the German question.
